plan.title: Drawing the sea: how medieval chart-makers worked
plan.businessGoal: Prepare the volunteer guides of the Aldermoor Maritime Museum (fictional client) to explain its new gallery of medieval charts before it opens: how a sea chart differs from a world map, how chart-makers built it, and how sailors used it.

audience.role: Volunteer gallery guides: retired teachers, former sailors and history students
audience.notes: At ease with a modern map and with compass directions. Most expect old maps to be clumsy versions of modern ones, and have never laid a course on a chart with a ruler and dividers. They will answer visitors' questions standing in front of the charts.

sources.title: Tony Campbell, "Portolan Charts from the Late Thirteenth Century to 1500", in J. B. Harley and David Woodward (eds), The History of Cartography, vol. 1, University of Chicago Press, 1987, chapter 19
David Woodward, "Medieval Mappaemundi", in J. B. Harley and David Woodward (eds), The History of Cartography, vol. 1, University of Chicago Press, 1987, chapter 18
Ramon J. Pujades i Bataller, Les cartes portolanes: la representació medieval d'una mar solcada, Institut Cartogràfic de Catalunya, 2007
Roel Nicolai, The Enigma of the Origin of Portolan Charts, Brill, 2016 (accuracy of the charts and their rotation)

objectives.statement: Tell a mappa mundi from a portolan chart by its purpose, its orientation and the way it was made, and explain to a visitor why a T-O map puts east at the top.
objectives.criterion: All the features of a chart sorted correctly in one question; one correct explanation

objectives.statement: Explain how a chart-maker built a portolan chart from compass bearings and distances, and use it to explain two features of the charts: the tilt of the Mediterranean and the names written across the land.
objectives.criterion: Two correct explanations out of two

objectives.statement: Lay a course between two harbours on a portolan chart: name the wind to steer from its rhumb lines, and measure the distance in miles against the scale.
objectives.criterion: Three voyages with the right wind and a distance within 10 %; one distance read from the scale

items.title: A map with no top
items.description: Hook: a visitor's question in front of a chart from Majorca, and the two ways medieval Europe drew the world.

lockedTexts.text: On the opening night of the gallery, a visitor stops in front of a chart drawn in Majorca around 1375 and frowns: “There is no north on this map, the names run in every direction, and Italy is lying down. Did they get it wrong?” They did not. Medieval Europe drew the world in two very different ways, for two very different readers, and the chart on the wall is a working tool, made for sailors and accurate enough to steer by.

items.title: The world as a book
items.description: Mappae mundi: the T-O diagram of Isidore of Seville (the Ocean, the three parts of the world, east at the top) and the Hereford map (about 1300, Jerusalem at the centre). Where "orienting" a map comes from.

items.title: The sea as a network
items.description: What a portolan chart is, compared with a mappa mundi on purpose, orientation, construction and use; an ungraded check sorting features.

lockedTexts.text: A portolan chart is a sea chart of the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, drawn on a single skin of vellum from the late thirteenth century onwards. It traces the coasts in remarkable detail, names hundreds of harbours and is criss-crossed by rhumb lines radiating from wind roses. It has no grid of latitude and longitude: as far as historians can tell, it was built from compass bearings and estimated distances between harbours.

items.title: In the chart-maker's workshop
items.description: Six stages of making a chart, as a figure that builds up while the learner reads: the skin, the hidden circle, the rhumb lines in three colours, the coasts from bearings and distances, the names, the scale and the colours. Why the Mediterranean is tilted. An ungraded check on the names.

items.title: At the chart table
items.description: The eight winds of the Mediterranean, explored on a wind rose; then three voyages on a 3D chart: choose the wind whose rhumb lines lead from one harbour to the other, open the dividers to the distance, and sail.

items.title: Ready for the gallery
items.description: Five questions a guide must be able to answer in front of the charts, and the score.

questions.stem: A visitor points at a chart in the gallery. Which features tell you it is a **portolan chart** rather than a mappa mundi? Select every one that applies.

options.text: Lines radiating across the sea from wind roses
options.feedback: Yes: the rhumb lines are the chart's working grid, for laying courses.

options.text: Jerusalem at the centre and east at the top
options.feedback: That is a mappa mundi: a picture of the world's history and faith, read from the top, where the east and Paradise lie.

options.text: Hundreds of harbour names along the coasts
options.feedback: Yes: a chart names every harbour a pilot might need, written across the land.
Yes: distances are measured with dividers against the scale. A mappa mundi has none.

options.text: Scenes from the Bible and the monsters of distant lands
options.feedback: Those fill the mappae mundi, which are encyclopaedias in pictures. A chart keeps the sea clear.

feedback.correct: Exactly: rhumb lines, harbour names and a scale make a working sea chart.
feedback.incorrect: Look for what a pilot needs: lines to steer by, harbours and a scale.

questions.stem: Why is the Mediterranean on a portolan chart turned about 9° anticlockwise, compared with a modern map?

options.text: It was drawn from compass bearings, and the compass pointed about 9° east of north
options.feedback: Right: the chart follows the compass. Steered with a compass, it still leads to the right harbour.

options.text: The skin shrank unevenly while it dried in the chart-maker's workshop
options.feedback: Skins do shrink a little, but unevenly, not by turning a whole sea by the same angle.

options.text: Chart-makers lifted the east, towards Jerusalem and the Garden of Eden
options.feedback: That is the logic of a mappa mundi, not of a chart for pilots.

options.text: They copied Ptolemy's coordinates, which put every coast too far north
options.feedback: The charts use no coordinates at all; Ptolemy's Geography reached Latin Europe only around 1400.

questions.stem: Why are the harbour names written across the land, at right angles to the coast?

options.text: To keep the coast clear on a chart read from every side: it has no top
options.feedback: Right: you turn the chart, not your head, and the coast itself stays readable.

options.text: To show which way the wind blows when you enter each of the harbours
options.feedback: Winds are read from the rhumb lines and the wind roses, not from the names.

options.text: To show how far inland each town lies, the longest names furthest away
options.feedback: The length of a name says nothing about distance: distances come from the scale.

options.text: Because the scribes of the chart workshops wrote from bottom to top
options.feedback: They wrote left to right, as we do: the names simply follow the coast round.

questions.stem: You open your dividers between two harbours, then lay them on the scale bar: they span **three and a half divisions**. Each division is 50 miles. How far apart are the harbours?

feedback.incorrect: Multiply the number of divisions by the miles in each: 3.5 × 50.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of divisions. Each one is worth 50 miles.
You counted three divisions. The dividers span half a division more: 25 miles.

questions.stem: Leaving Valencia for Majorca, you lay your ruler between the two harbours. The rhumb line that runs parallel to it is ruled in black and points towards the rising sun. Which wind do you steer by?

options.feedback: Right: black lines are the eight principal winds, and Levante is the wind of the rising sun, the east.
Ponente is the wind of the setting sun: you would sail west, away from Majorca.
Greco is north-east: the line would lead you to Catalonia's coast, not to Majorca.
Scirocco is south-east: the line would pass well south of Majorca.

spacing: D+2: explain one chart of the gallery to a peer
D+7: answer three visitor questions by email
D+21: first tour, observed by the curator
